items.stem: What is oxidation in terms of electrons?
items.answer: loss of electrons
items.markingKey: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain.

items.stem: Explain why the reaction of magnesium with oxygen is described as oxidation in two different ways.
items.answer: Magnesium gains oxygen to form MgO; also each Mg atom loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: gains oxygen; 1 mark: loses electrons [2]

items.stem: Explain why oxidation and reduction must always happen together.
items.answer: Electrons lost by one substance must be gained by another (or oxygen removed from one is added to another).

items.stem: In the reaction Zn(s) + Pb²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Pb(s), which statement is correct?
options: Zn gains electrons and is reduced.
Pb²⁺ loses electrons and is oxidised.
Zn loses electrons and is oxidised.
Pb²⁺ gains electrons and is oxidised.
items.answer: Zn loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb (reduction).

items.stem: For the reaction Zn(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + H₂(g), identify the species oxidised and the species reduced, explaining your answer in terms of electrons.
items.answer: Zn is oxidised (loses electrons: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻); H⁺ is reduced (gains electrons: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Zn oxidised; 1 mark: H⁺ reduced; 1 mark: electron loss/gain explanation [3]

items.stem: For the reaction Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), identify the species oxidised and the species reduced, explaining your answer in terms of electrons. Write the two half-equations.
items.answer: Fe is oxidised (loses electrons: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻); Cu²⁺ is reduced (gains electrons: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Fe oxidised; 1 mark: Cu²⁺ reduced; 1 mark: electron loss/gain explanation; 1 mark: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; 1 mark: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu [5]

items.stem: Nadia studies two reactions. Reaction 1: Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(l). Reaction 2: 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s). (a) Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons. (b) Identify the oxidising agent in reaction 2. (c) Explain why reaction 2 is a redox reaction even though no oxygen is involved.
items.answer: (a) oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain of electrons (b) Cl₂ (c) electrons are transferred from Na to Cl₂

items.stem: Isla studies two reactions. Reaction 1: ZnO(s) + C(s) → Zn(s) + CO(g). Reaction 2: 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s). (a) Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in reaction 1. (b) Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons. (c) Identify the oxidising agent in reaction 2.
items.answer: (a) oxidised: carbon; reduced: zinc oxide (b) oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain of electrons (c) Cl₂
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: What is reduction in terms of oxygen?
items.answer: loss of oxygen
items.markingKey: A substance that loses oxygen is reduced.

items.stem: What is a redox reaction?
options: a reaction in which oxidation and reduction take place at the same time
a reaction that only involves oxygen
a reaction in which a precipitate forms
items.answer: a reaction in which oxidation and reduction take place at the same time
items.markingKey: Electrons lost by one species are gained by another.

items.stem: Explain why the reaction of chlorine with potassium bromide is a redox reaction even though no oxygen is involved.
items.answer: Bromide ions lose electrons (oxidised) to form bromine; chlorine gains electrons (reduced) to form chloride ions.

items.stem: A student says, "In Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, iron is oxidised because it changes." Explain the error.
items.answer: Iron(III) oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced; carbon monoxide gains oxygen and is oxidised.

items.stem: Explain why the reaction ZnO(s) + C(s) → Zn(s) + CO(g) is a redox reaction.
items.answer: Zinc oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced; carbon gains oxygen, so it is oxidised. Both happen at once.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: reduced species with reason; 1 mark: oxidised species with reason [2]

items.stem: Explain why the reaction 2Mg(s) + CO₂(g) → 2MgO(s) + C(s) is a redox reaction.
items.answer: Carbon dioxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced; magnesium gains oxygen, so it is oxidised. Both happen at once.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: reduced species with reason; 1 mark: oxidised species with reason [2]

items.stem: For the reaction Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g), identify the species oxidised and the species reduced, explaining your answer in terms of electrons.
items.answer: Mg is oxidised (loses electrons: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻); H⁺ is reduced (gains electrons: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Mg oxidised; 1 mark: H⁺ reduced; 1 mark: electron loss/gain explanation [3]

items.stem: In the reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which statement is correct?
options: Zn gains electrons and is reduced.
Zn gains electrons and is oxidised.
Zn loses electrons and is oxidised.
Cu²⁺ gains electrons and is oxidised.
items.answer: Zn loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction).

items.stem: In the reaction Mg(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s), which statement is correct?
options: Mg gains electrons and is reduced.
Mg gains electrons and is oxidised.
Mg loses electrons and is oxidised.
Ag⁺ loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.answer: Mg loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag (reduction).

items.stem: In the reaction 2Al(s) + 3Cu²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Cu(s), which statement is correct?
options: Al loses electrons and is oxidised.
Cu²⁺ loses electrons and is oxidised.
Al gains electrons and is oxidised.
Al gains electrons and is reduced.
items.answer: Al loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ (oxidation); Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction).

items.stem: For the reaction Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq), identify the species oxidised and the species reduced, explaining your answer in terms of electrons.
items.answer: Br⁻ is oxidised (loses electrons: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻); Cl₂ is reduced (gains electrons: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Br⁻ oxidised; 1 mark: Cl₂ reduced; 1 mark: electron loss/gain explanation [3]

items.stem: For the reaction Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq), identify the species oxidised and the species reduced, explaining your answer in terms of electrons. Write the two half-equations.
items.answer: Br⁻ is oxidised (loses electrons: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻); Cl₂ is reduced (gains electrons: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Br⁻ oxidised; 1 mark: Cl₂ reduced; 1 mark: electron loss/gain explanation; 1 mark: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻; 1 mark: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ [5]

items.stem: Ethan studies two reactions. Reaction 1: Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(l) + 3CO₂(g). Reaction 2: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g). (a) Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in reaction 1. (b) Write the two half-equations for reaction 2.
items.answer: (a) oxidised: carbon monoxide; reduced: iron(III) oxide (b) Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Jonas studies two reactions. Reaction 1: Fe₂O₃(s) + 3C(s) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO(g). Reaction 2: 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s). (a) Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in reaction 1. (b) Write the two half-equations for reaction 2.
items.answer: (a) oxidised: carbon; reduced: iron(III) oxide (b) Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Lina studies two reactions. Reaction 1: 2CuO(s) + C(s) → 2Cu(s) + CO₂(g). Reaction 2: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g). (a) Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in reaction 1. (b) Write the two half-equations for reaction 2. (c) Identify the oxidising agent in reaction 2.
items.answer: (a) oxidised: carbon; reduced: copper(II) oxide (b) Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (c) H⁺
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: What is the oxidation number of any uncombined element?
items.markingKey: Elements (e.g. O₂, Fe) have oxidation number 0.

items.stem: Explain why the sum of the oxidation numbers in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻, is −2.
items.answer: The sum of oxidation numbers in an ion equals the charge on the ion: S (+6) + 4 × O (−2) = −2.

items.stem: Explain why Roman numerals are needed in the names of iron compounds but not in the names of sodium compounds.
items.answer: Iron (a transition element) has variable oxidation numbers (+2 and +3), so the numeral shows which ion is present; sodium is always +1.

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of the stated element in each species: Mn in KMnO₄; Mn in MnO₄⁻.
items.answer: Mn in KMnO₄: +7; Mn in MnO₄⁻: +7
items.markingKey: Mn in KMnO₄: +7; Mn in MnO₄⁻: +7. 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of the stated element in each species: N in N₂O; Cu in Cu₂O; S in H₂SO₄.
items.answer: N in N₂O: +1; Cu in Cu₂O: +1; S in H₂SO₄: +6
items.markingKey: N in N₂O: +1; Cu in Cu₂O: +1; S in H₂SO₄: +6. 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Amara is given a bottle labelled iron(II) hydroxide and also studies the species H₂SO₄ and Cr₂O₃. (a) State what the Roman numeral in the name tells you. (b) Deduce the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₃. (c) State the rules you used to deduce oxidation numbers.
items.answer: (a) the oxidation number of the metal/element is +2 (b) 3 (c) elements 0; O −2; H +1; sum = 0 for compounds or = charge for ions

items.stem: What is the usual oxidation number of oxygen in its compounds?
items.markingKey: Oxygen is usually −2 (except peroxides).

items.stem: Explain, using oxidation numbers, why 2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻ is a redox reaction.
items.answer: Fe increases from +2 to +3 (oxidised); Cl decreases from 0 to −1 (reduced).

items.stem: Explain how the name potassium manganate(VII) shows the oxidation number of manganese in KMnO₄.
items.answer: The (VII) shows Mn is +7: +1 (K) + 7 + 4 × (−2) = 0.

items.stem: Explain how the name copper(II) oxide relates to the formula CuO.
items.answer: The numeral (II) is the oxidation number (+2) of the copper in the compound; the other ions/atoms balance this so the total is zero.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: numeral = oxidation number; 1 mark: charge balance shown [2]

items.stem: Explain how the name potassium manganate(VII) relates to the formula KMnO₄.
items.answer: The numeral (VII) is the oxidation number (+7) of the manganate in the compound; the other ions/atoms balance this so the total is zero.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: numeral = oxidation number; 1 mark: charge balance shown [2]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of the stated element in each species: C in CO; S in SO₂Cl₂.
items.answer: C in CO: +2; S in SO₂Cl₂: +6
items.markingKey: C in CO: +2; S in SO₂Cl₂: +6. 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Use oxidation numbers to show that Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ is a redox reaction. Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.
items.answer: Fe: +3 → 0; C: +2 → +4. Oxidising agent: Fe₂O₃; reducing agent: CO.
items.markingKey: Fe +3 → 0; C +2 → +4 [2]; increase = oxidation, decrease = reduction [1]; agents [1]

items.stem: Use oxidation numbers to show that 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃ is a redox reaction. Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.
items.answer: S: +4 → +6; O: 0 → −2. Oxidising agent: O₂; reducing agent: SO₂.
items.markingKey: S +4 → +6; O 0 → −2 [2]; increase = oxidation, decrease = reduction [1]; agents [1]

items.stem: Jonas is given a bottle labelled chromium(III) oxide and also studies the species KMnO₄ and NO₃⁻. (a) Deduce the oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄. (b) Deduce the oxidation number of N in NO₃⁻. (c) State the rules you used to deduce oxidation numbers.
items.answer: (a) 7 (b) 5 (c) elements 0; O −2; H +1; sum = 0 for compounds or = charge for ions

items.stem: Ana is given a bottle labelled tin(IV) chloride and also studies the species SO₃²⁻ and HCl. (a) Write the formula of the compound in the bottle. (b) State what the Roman numeral in the name tells you. (c) Deduce the oxidation number of Cl in HCl. (d) Define oxidation in terms of oxidation number. (e) State the rules you used to deduce oxidation numbers.
items.answer: (a) SnCl₄ (b) the oxidation number of the metal/element is +4 (c) -1 (d) an increase in oxidation number (e) elements 0; O −2; H +1; sum = 0 for compounds or = charge for ions

items.stem: What is an oxidising agent?
options: a substance that gives away electrons
a substance that oxidises another substance and is itself reduced
items.answer: a substance that oxidises another substance and is itself reduced
items.markingKey: It accepts electrons.

items.stem: Explain why potassium iodide is used to test for an oxidising agent.
items.answer: An oxidising agent removes electrons from iodide ions, forming iodine; the colourless solution turns brown.

items.stem: Explain why acidified potassium manganate(VII) turns colourless when sulfur dioxide is bubbled through it.
items.answer: Sulfur dioxide is a reducing agent: it gives electrons to the manganate(VII) ions, reducing them from purple MnO₄⁻ to colourless Mn²⁺.

items.stem: Solution A is tested: acidified potassium manganate(VII) changes from purple to colourless; aqueous potassium iodide shows no change. What does this show about A?
items.answer: It is a reducing agent.
items.markingKey: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) changes from purple to colourless; aqueous potassium iodide shows no change → reducing agent.

items.stem: Noah, a student in Santiago, tests solution A (iron(II) sulfate solution) with two reagents: acidified potassium manganate(VII) changes from purple to colourless; aqueous potassium iodide shows no change. Deduce whether A is an oxidising or a reducing agent and explain the colour change in terms of electron transfer.
items.answer: Reducing agent. Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺: A gives electrons to MnO₄⁻ ions, which are reduced to colourless Mn²⁺.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct deduction; 1 mark: identifies the colour change; 1 mark: electron transfer explanation [3]

items.stem: Lina has two unlabelled solutions, P and Q. One is iron(II) sulfate solution and the other is sodium chlorate(I) (bleach) solution. Acidified potassium manganate(VII) and aqueous potassium iodide are available. (a) Describe how the two reagents can be used to identify which solution is the reducing agent. (b) Explain the colour change with potassium iodide in terms of electrons.
items.answer: (a) add acidified KMnO₄: the reducing agent turns it from purple to colourless (b) the oxidising agent removes electrons from iodide ions: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reagent; 1 mark colour change [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: What colour change is seen when acidified potassium manganate(VII) reacts with a reducing agent?
items.answer: purple to colourless
items.markingKey: MnO₄⁻ (purple) is reduced to Mn²⁺ (colourless).

items.stem: In the reaction Zn(s) + Pb²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Pb(s), what is the oxidising agent?
items.answer: Pb²⁺
items.markingKey: Zn loses electrons (reducing agent); Pb²⁺ gains electrons (oxidising agent).

items.stem: Explain why an oxidising agent is itself reduced.
items.answer: It gains the electrons that it removes from the substance it oxidises.

items.stem: Explain why a substance cannot be both an oxidising agent and the substance oxidised in the same reaction step.
items.answer: The oxidising agent gains electrons (is reduced) while the substance oxidised loses electrons; one species cannot both gain and lose the same electrons.

items.stem: In the reaction 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s), explain which species is the oxidising agent and which is the reducing agent.
items.answer: Cl₂ is the oxidising agent: it gains electrons (Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻) and is reduced. Na is the reducing agent: it loses electrons (Na → Na⁺ + e⁻) and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: oxidising agent; 1 mark: reducing agent; 1 mark: half-equations or electron explanation [3]

items.stem: Solution Z is tested: aqueous potassium iodide changes from colourless to brown; acidified potassium manganate(VII) stays purple. What does this show about Z?
items.answer: It is a oxidising agent.
items.markingKey: Aqueous potassium iodide changes from colourless to brown; acidified potassium manganate(VII) stays purple → oxidising agent.

items.stem: Solution Z is tested: acidified potassium manganate(VII) changes from purple to colourless; aqueous potassium iodide shows no change. What does this show about Z?
items.answer: It is a reducing agent.
items.markingKey: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) changes from purple to colourless; aqueous potassium iodide shows no change → reducing agent.

items.stem: Ethan, a student in Doha, tests solution Z (ethanol (warm)) with two reagents: acidified potassium manganate(VII) changes from purple to colourless; aqueous potassium iodide shows no change. Deduce whether Z is an oxidising or a reducing agent and explain the colour change in terms of electron transfer.
items.answer: Reducing agent. ethanol is oxidised: Z gives electrons to MnO₄⁻ ions, which are reduced to colourless Mn²⁺.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct deduction; 1 mark: identifies the colour change; 1 mark: electron transfer explanation [3]

items.stem: Ravi has two unlabelled solutions, P and Q. One is sodium sulfite solution and the other is chlorine water. Acidified potassium manganate(VII) and aqueous potassium iodide are available. (a) Describe the result expected when aqueous potassium iodide is added to the oxidising agent. (b) State what happens to the oxidation number of manganese when manganate(VII) reacts with the reducing agent. (c) Explain why sodium sulfite solution is described as a reducing agent.
items.answer: (a) colourless to brown (iodine formed) (b) decreases from +7 to +2 (reduced) (c) SO₃²⁻ is oxidised to SO₄²⁻: it loses electrons and reduces the other substance

items.stem: Lucas has two unlabelled solutions, P and Q. One is sulfur dioxide solution and the other is iron(III) chloride solution. Acidified potassium manganate(VII) and aqueous potassium iodide are available. (a) Describe the result expected when aqueous potassium iodide is added to the oxidising agent. (b) Explain the colour change with potassium iodide in terms of electrons. (c) Explain why sulfur dioxide solution is described as a reducing agent.
items.answer: (a) colourless to brown (iodine formed) (b) the oxidising agent removes electrons from iodide ions: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻ (c) SO₂ is oxidised to sulfate: it loses electrons and reduces the other substance

items.stem: In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which species is reduced?
items.answer: Cu²⁺
items.markingKey: Cu²⁺ gains two electrons.

items.stem: Explain why the reaction 2PbO(s) + C(s) → 2Pb(s) + CO₂(g) is a redox reaction.
items.answer: Lead(II) oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced; carbon gains oxygen, so it is oxidised. Both happen at once.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: reduced species with reason; 1 mark: oxidised species with reason [2]

items.stem: Leila writes that in the reaction Zn(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + H₂(g), "H⁺ is oxidised because it gains electrons." Identify the error and correct it.
items.answer: Gaining electrons is reduction: H⁺ is reduced (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂); Zn is oxidised (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: gain of electrons = reduction; 1 mark: correct identification [2]

items.stem: In the reaction Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which statement is correct?
options: Fe loses electrons and is oxidised.
Cu²⁺ loses electrons and is oxidised.
Cu²⁺ gains electrons and is oxidised.
Fe gains electrons and is oxidised.
items.answer: Fe loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction).

items.stem: In the reaction Cl₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + I₂(aq), which statement is correct?
options: Cl₂ loses electrons and is oxidised.
Cl₂ gains electrons and is oxidised.
I⁻ gains electrons and is oxidised.
I⁻ loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.answer: I⁻ loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ (reduction).

items.stem: In the reaction 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s), which statement is correct?
options: Cl₂ loses electrons and is oxidised.
Na gains electrons and is oxidised.
Cl₂ gains electrons and is oxidised.
Na loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.answer: Na loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ (oxidation); Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ (reduction).

items.stem: Sipho studies two reactions. Reaction 1: Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(l). Reaction 2: 2Al(s) + 3Cu²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Cu(s). (a) Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in reaction 1. (b) Identify the oxidising agent in reaction 2. (c) Explain why reaction 2 is a redox reaction even though no oxygen is involved.
items.answer: (a) oxidised: aluminium; reduced: iron(III) oxide (b) Cu²⁺ (c) electrons are transferred from Al to Cu²⁺
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Aisha studies two reactions. Reaction 1: Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(l). Reaction 2: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). (a) Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in reaction 1. (b) Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons.
items.answer: (a) oxidised: aluminium; reduced: iron(III) oxide (b) oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain of electrons
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: What does the Roman numeral in iron(III) chloride show?
options: the oxidation number of iron is +3
items.answer: the oxidation number of iron is +3
items.markingKey: Roman numeral = oxidation number of the metal.

items.stem: Explain how the name iron(II) chloride relates to the formula FeCl₂.
items.answer: The numeral (II) is the oxidation number (+2) of the iron in the compound; the other ions/atoms balance this so the total is zero.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: numeral = oxidation number; 1 mark: charge balance shown [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how the name potassium manganate(VII) shows the oxidation number of manganese in KMnO₄. (b) Explain, using oxidation numbers, why 2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻ is a redox reaction.
items.answer: (a) The (VII) shows Mn is +7: +1 (K) + 7 + 4 × (−2) = 0. (b) Fe increases from +2 to +3 (oxidised); Cl decreases from 0 to −1 (reduced).

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of the stated element in each species: Cl in Cl₂O₇; Cu in CuO.
items.answer: Cl in Cl₂O₇: +7; Cu in CuO: +2
items.markingKey: Cl in Cl₂O₇: +7; Cu in CuO: +2. 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of the stated element in each species: C in CO₂; S in SO₃²⁻; S in SO₃.
items.answer: C in CO₂: +4; S in SO₃²⁻: +4; S in SO₃: +6
items.markingKey: C in CO₂: +4; S in SO₃²⁻: +4; S in SO₃: +6. 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Sipho is given a bottle labelled lead(IV) oxide and also studies the species CO₃²⁻ and SO₂Cl₂. (a) State what the Roman numeral in the name tells you. (b) Deduce the oxidation number of C in CO₃²⁻. (c) Deduce the oxidation number of S in SO₂Cl₂. (d) State the rules you used to deduce oxidation numbers.
items.answer: (a) the oxidation number of the metal/element is +4 (b) 4 (c) 6 (d) elements 0; O −2; H +1; sum = 0 for compounds or = charge for ions

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In the reaction CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, what is the reducing agent? (b) State the reagent used to test for a reducing agent.
items.answer: (a) hydrogen (b) acidified potassium manganate(VII)
items.markingKey: (a) H₂ removes oxygen from CuO and is itself oxidised. (b) [1]

items.stem: In the reaction Zn(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + H₂(g), explain which species is the oxidising agent and which is the reducing agent.
items.answer: H⁺ is the oxidising agent: it gains electrons (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂) and is reduced. Zn is the reducing agent: it loses electrons (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: oxidising agent with reason; 1 mark: reducing agent with reason [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why potassium iodide is used to test for an oxidising agent. (b) Explain why a substance cannot be both an oxidising agent and the substance oxidised in the same reaction step.
items.answer: (a) An oxidising agent removes electrons from iodide ions, forming iodine; the colourless solution turns brown. (b) The oxidising agent gains electrons (is reduced) while the substance oxidised loses electrons; one species cannot both gain and lose the same electrons.

items.stem: Solution R is tested: aqueous potassium iodide changes from colourless to brown; acidified potassium manganate(VII) stays purple. What does this show about R?
items.answer: It is a oxidising agent.
items.markingKey: Aqueous potassium iodide changes from colourless to brown; acidified potassium manganate(VII) stays purple → oxidising agent.

items.stem: Lina, a student in Lisbon, tests solution K (chlorine water) with two reagents: aqueous potassium iodide changes from colourless to brown; acidified potassium manganate(VII) stays purple. Deduce whether K is an oxidising or a reducing agent and explain the colour change in terms of electron transfer.
items.answer: Oxidising agent. Cl₂ is reduced to Cl⁻: K takes electrons from I⁻ ions, which are oxidised to brown I₂.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct deduction; 1 mark: identifies the colour change; 1 mark: electron transfer explanation [3]

items.stem: Noah has two unlabelled solutions, P and Q. One is sulfur dioxide solution and the other is acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Acidified potassium manganate(VII) and aqueous potassium iodide are available. (a) Describe how the two reagents can be used to identify which solution is the reducing agent. (b) Describe the result expected when aqueous potassium iodide is added to the oxidising agent. (c) Explain the colour change with potassium iodide in terms of electrons. (d) Suggest why the potassium manganate(VII) must be acidified.
items.answer: (a) add acidified KMnO₄: the reducing agent turns it from purple to colourless (b) colourless to brown (iodine formed) (c) the oxidising agent removes electrons from iodide ions: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻ (d) H⁺ ions are needed for the reduction of MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reagent; 1 mark colour change [2] (b) [1] (c) [2] (d) [1]

items.stem: State the meaning of OIL RIG.
items.answer: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons)

items.stem: Zara writes that in the reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), "Cu²⁺ is oxidised because it gains electrons." Identify the error and correct it.
items.answer: Gaining electrons is reduction: Cu²⁺ is reduced (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu); Zn is oxidised (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: gain of electrons = reduction; 1 mark: correct identification [2]

items.stem: Explain why the reaction PbO(s) + H₂(g) → Pb(s) + H₂O(l) is a redox reaction.
items.answer: Lead(II) oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced; hydrogen gains oxygen, so it is oxidised. Both happen at once.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: reduced species with reason; 1 mark: oxidised species with reason [2]

items.stem: In the reaction Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which statement is correct?
options: Mg gains electrons and is oxidised.
Mg gains electrons and is reduced.
Mg loses electrons and is oxidised.
Cu²⁺ loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.answer: Mg loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction).

items.stem: In the reaction Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s), which statement is correct?
options: Ag⁺ loses electrons and is oxidised.
Cu gains electrons and is reduced.
Ag⁺ gains electrons and is oxidised.
Cu loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.answer: Cu loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag (reduction).

items.stem: In the reaction Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq), which statement is correct?
options: I⁻ loses electrons and is oxidised.
Br₂ loses electrons and is oxidised.
I⁻ gains electrons and is oxidised.
Br₂ gains electrons and is oxidised.
items.answer: I⁻ loses electrons and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Br₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Br⁻ (reduction).

items.stem: Jonas studies two reactions. Reaction 1: 2CuO(s) + C(s) → 2Cu(s) + CO₂(g). Reaction 2: Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). (a) Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in reaction 1. (b) Identify the oxidising agent in reaction 2. (c) Explain why reaction 2 is a redox reaction even though no oxygen is involved.
items.answer: (a) oxidised: carbon; reduced: copper(II) oxide (b) Cu²⁺ (c) electrons are transferred from Fe to Cu²⁺
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Elena studies two reactions. Reaction 1: Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(l) + 3CO₂(g). Reaction 2: Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s). (a) Define oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen. (b) Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in reaction 1.
items.answer: (a) oxidation: gain of oxygen; reduction: loss of oxygen (b) oxidised: carbon monoxide; reduced: iron(III) oxide
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: In terms of oxidation number, what happens to a species that is oxidised?
options: Its oxidation number stays the same.
items.answer: Its oxidation number increases.
items.markingKey: Oxidation: increase in oxidation number.

items.stem: Explain how the name iron(II) sulfate relates to the formula FeSO₄.
items.answer: The numeral (II) is the oxidation number (+2) of the iron in the compound; the other ions/atoms balance this so the total is zero.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: numeral = oxidation number; 1 mark: charge balance shown [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain, using oxidation numbers, why 2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻ is a redox reaction. (b) Explain why the sum of the oxidation numbers in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻, is −2.
items.answer: (a) Fe increases from +2 to +3 (oxidised); Cl decreases from 0 to −1 (reduced). (b) The sum of oxidation numbers in an ion equals the charge on the ion: S (+6) + 4 × O (−2) = −2.

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of the stated element in each species: Cl in NaClO₃; N in NO.
items.answer: Cl in NaClO₃: +5; N in NO: +2
items.markingKey: Cl in NaClO₃: +5; N in NO: +2. 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of the stated element in each species: I in KIO₃; N in NO; S in SO₃²⁻.
items.answer: I in KIO₃: +5; N in NO: +2; S in SO₃²⁻: +4
items.markingKey: I in KIO₃: +5; N in NO: +2; S in SO₃²⁻: +4. 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Omar is given a bottle labelled iron(III) sulfate and also studies the species Cr₂O₃ and NO. (a) State what the Roman numeral in the name tells you. (b) Deduce the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₃. (c) Define oxidation in terms of oxidation number. (d) State the rules you used to deduce oxidation numbers.
items.answer: (a) the oxidation number of the metal/element is +3 (b) 3 (c) an increase in oxidation number (d) elements 0; O −2; H +1; sum = 0 for compounds or = charge for ions

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In the reaction CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, what is the reducing agent? (b) What colour change is seen when aqueous potassium iodide reacts with an oxidising agent?
items.answer: (a) hydrogen (b) colourless to brown
items.markingKey: (a) H₂ removes oxygen from CuO and is itself oxidised. (b) I⁻ is oxidised to I₂ (brown in solution).

items.stem: In the reaction Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), explain which species is the oxidising agent and which is the reducing agent.
items.answer: Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent: it gains electrons (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu) and is reduced. Fe is the reducing agent: it loses electrons (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: oxidising agent with reason; 1 mark: reducing agent with reason [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why potassium iodide is used to test for an oxidising agent. (b) Explain why an oxidising agent is itself reduced.
items.answer: (a) An oxidising agent removes electrons from iodide ions, forming iodine; the colourless solution turns brown. (b) It gains the electrons that it removes from the substance it oxidises.

items.stem: Solution J is tested: aqueous potassium iodide changes from colourless to brown; acidified potassium manganate(VII) stays purple. What does this show about J?
items.answer: It is a oxidising agent.
items.markingKey: Aqueous potassium iodide changes from colourless to brown; acidified potassium manganate(VII) stays purple → oxidising agent.

items.stem: Ines, a student in Auckland, tests solution Y (potassium iodide solution) with two reagents: acidified potassium manganate(VII) changes from purple to colourless; aqueous potassium iodide shows no change. Deduce whether Y is an oxidising or a reducing agent and explain the colour change in terms of electron transfer.
items.answer: Reducing agent. I⁻ is oxidised to I₂: Y gives electrons to MnO₄⁻ ions, which are reduced to colourless Mn²⁺.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct deduction; 1 mark: identifies the colour change; 1 mark: electron transfer explanation [3]

items.stem: Mei has two unlabelled solutions, P and Q. One is iron(II) sulfate solution and the other is iron(III) chloride solution. Acidified potassium manganate(VII) and aqueous potassium iodide are available. (a) Explain the colour change with potassium iodide in terms of electrons. (b) State what happens to the oxidation number of manganese when manganate(VII) reacts with the reducing agent. (c) Explain why iron(II) sulfate solution is described as a reducing agent. (d) Suggest why the potassium manganate(VII) must be acidified.
items.answer: (a) the oxidising agent removes electrons from iodide ions: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻ (b) decreases from +7 to +2 (reduced) (c) Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺: it loses electrons and reduces the other substance (d) H⁺ ions are needed for the reduction of MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺
